# Internal Review: "Sparse Routing for Efficient Retrieval"

**Reviewed artifact:** `experiments/feynman-eval-case-study/fixtures/mini-eval-paper.md` (26 lines, 6 sections)
**Review mode:** Adversarial empirical-rigor / evaluation-validity audit
**Review date:** 2026-11-13
**Recommendation:** Major revision; the central claims are not currently supported by the reported evidence.

---

## Summary

The paper proposes SparseRoute, a learned top-k routing layer over 64 experts, applied to long-context retrieval. The claimed result is an accuracy improvement from 80.1% to 80.3% together with a halving of latency (40 ms → 20 ms), evaluated on a held-out split of 100 examples from an unnamed benchmark, against a baseline the authors trained themselves. The paper asserts a new state of the art and recommends production adoption.

The contribution is presented at a level of detail below what is needed to assess it. There is no named dataset, no published comparison, no ablation, no confidence interval, no per-seed result, no latency measurement protocol, and no related-work positioning. Most consequentially, the two headline accuracy numbers are arithmetically impossible under the evaluation protocol the paper itself states (100 examples, 3 seeds, mean over seeds), and the reported effect is roughly two orders of magnitude below the resolution of that evaluation design. The paper is best read as an early internal result note; in its current form it does not support its abstract, its results interpretation, or its conclusion.

## Strengths

- **[S1]** The paper reports latency alongside accuracy rather than accuracy alone (Results table). For an efficiency-motivated routing method this is the right pair of metrics to report, and many short papers omit latency entirely.
- **[S2]** The evaluation uses a held-out split rather than reporting training-set accuracy (Evaluation section). This is a genuine, if minimal, attempt at a clean generalization estimate.
- **[S3]** The authors ran 3 seeds and report the mean rather than the best seed (Evaluation section). Reporting a seed mean is the correct instinct and is preferable to max-over-seeds reporting, which is common and misleading.
- **[S4]** The baseline is described as trained "with the same budget" (Evaluation section). Attempting compute parity with the baseline is the right control to attempt, even though the execution is under-specified (see W4).
- **[S5]** The claims in the Abstract and Results are numerically consistent with the Results table (80.1 → 80.3; 40 → 20 ms). There is no internal contradiction between prose and table, which is not nothing in a short draft.

## Weaknesses

- **[W1] FATAL — The "state of the art" claim has no referent.** The Abstract states the method "establishes a new state of the art," and the Conclusion repeats it. SOTA is a comparative claim against the best published results on a named benchmark. The paper names no benchmark, cites no published system, and compares only to a baseline the authors trained. A self-trained baseline is not a SOTA comparison under any reading; it is at best an internal ablation. There is no evidence in the paper that any external result was consulted.

- **[W2] FATAL — The reported accuracy means are arithmetically impossible under the stated protocol, and the effect size is below the design's resolution.** The Evaluation section states a 100-example held-out split, 3 seeds, and mean accuracy over seeds. Per-seed accuracy on 100 examples must be an integer count out of 100; the mean of three such values must therefore be a multiple of 1/300 ≈ 0.333 percentage points. The reported means, 80.1% and 80.3%, correspond to 240.3/300 and 240.9/300 — non-integer numerators, hence unattainable. Either the split is not 100 examples, or more than 3 runs are averaged, or the numbers were not produced by the described procedure. Any of these possibilities is a serious reporting problem, and the paper does not acknowledge it. Separately, a 0.2-point difference on 100 examples is 0.2 example predictions per seed (0.6 across three seeds), whereas the binomial standard error at p ≈ 0.8, n = 100 is ≈ 4.0 points and the approximate 95% minimum detectable unpaired difference is ≈ 11 points. The claimed gain is roughly 1/20th of one standard error. With no confidence interval (explicitly declined in the Evaluation section), the result is indistinguishable from seed noise.

- **[W3] FATAL — The 2× latency claim has no measurement protocol and a plausible confound.** The paper reports "40 ms" and "20 ms" with no hardware, batch size, sequence length, retrieval corpus size, percentile (mean vs p50 vs p95), warm-up, or repeat count. A routing layer over 64 experts adds computation and memory traffic; the paper never explains the mechanism by which adding a router halves end-to-end latency. The most likely explanation is that routing reduces the number of retrieved passages or tokens processed downstream — which would simultaneously change the accuracy task and invalidate the head-to-head accuracy comparison. This confound is not discussed anywhere. As written, neither the 2× nor the accuracy delta is attributable to the stated cause.

- **[W4] MAJOR — The baseline is under-specified and the parity claim is undefined.** "A baseline we trained ourselves with the same budget" does not identify the baseline architecture, whether it shares the retriever, whether it was tuned over the same hyperparameter grid, or what "budget" means (epochs, FLOPs, wall-clock, GPU-hours). Training a baseline for 10 epochs at a single learning rate (Method) is not evidence of a tuned baseline. An under-tuned self-trained baseline is the single most common way a small routing gain is manufactured. Without tuning-parity details, the 0.2-point delta has no clear interpretation even before the statistics are considered.

- **[W5] MAJOR — No ablation isolates the router.** The Method introduces three design choices — a learned router, top-k selection, and 64 experts — and the Results report only the full system versus one baseline. There is no ablation of the router (e.g., fixed/uniform routing, random top-k), no sweep over k, and no sweep over expert count. The paper therefore cannot attribute the measured difference to routing rather than to parameter count, changed retrieval depth, or added capacity. The number 64 is asserted without justification or sensitivity analysis.

- **[W6] MAJOR — "The gain is consistent across seeds" is unfalsifiable as reported.** The paper states results "were stable" and the gain is "consistent across seeds" while explicitly withholding per-seed numbers and confidence intervals. Consistency across seeds cannot be assessed from a single mean per method. This is a claim about variance made in the absence of any variance reporting — the strongest form of unsupported stability claim. If the per-seed counts were, e.g., 80/81/80 versus 81/80/80, the "consistent" gain would be an artifact of averaging.

- **[W7] MAJOR — Evaluation-set provenance and contamination are unaddressed.** "A held-out split of 100 examples from the benchmark" does not name the benchmark, the corpus, the split construction, or the deduplication procedure against training data. It is also unstated whether the 100 examples were used for any model or router selection (top-k, expert count, early stopping). A 100-example split is small enough that even inadvertent peeking would dominate the reported effect. For a retrieval benchmark, train/test passage overlap is a known and severe contamination channel; nothing in the paper rules it out.

- **[W8] MAJOR — No related work and no novelty positioning.** The paper contains zero citations. Sparse routing over experts and routing for retrieval are both well-established lines of work (e.g., sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layers, Shazeer et al., 2017; retrieval-augmented and routed-retrieval systems). A reader cannot determine what is new here relative to that literature, and the paper makes no attempt to distinguish its router from standard top-k MoE routing. The absence of related work is not a formatting omission in a paper whose entire claim is novelty.

- **[W9] MINOR — Training and task specification are insufficient for reproduction.** The Method gives 10 epochs, Adam, lr = 1e-4, and nothing else: no dataset or corpus size, batch size, sequence length, warm-up/schedule, weight decay, hardware, total compute, or definition of "long context" (how many tokens?). The learning rate is stated as a single value with no indication that it was tuned. None of this is reproducible as written.

- **[W10] MINOR — Spurious precision.** Reporting 80.1% and 80.3% implies a measurement resolution of 0.1 points. On 100 examples the natural resolution is 1 point per seed. The extra digit conveys confidence the design does not have and is the surface symptom of W2.

- **[W11] MINOR — The Conclusion outruns the evidence by a wide margin.** "Should be adopted in production systems" is a deployment recommendation based on a 100-example offline evaluation with no cost model, no failure analysis, no distribution-shift analysis, and no serving benchmark. No limitations section exists to temper any of this.

## Questions for Authors

- **[Q1]** Please provide the per-seed accuracy as integer counts (k/100) for both Baseline and SparseRoute. This is the minimum needed to check W2 and W6.
- **[Q2]** Given 100 examples and 3 seeds, how were means of 80.1% and 80.3% computed? Is the split actually 100 examples, and is the mean over exactly 3 runs?
- **[Q3]** What is the benchmark, and how was the 100-example held-out split constructed? Was it deduplicated against training passages, and was it used for any hyperparameter or design selection?
- **[Q4]** What exactly is the baseline architecture, and what does "same budget" mean operationally? Was the baseline tuned over a comparable hyperparameter grid?
- **[Q5]** What is the latency measurement protocol — hardware, batch size, context length, corpus size, statistic (mean/p50/p95), warm-up, and number of repeats? Are the 40 ms and 20 ms single measurements?
- **[Q6]** Does routing change the number of retrieved passages or tokens passed to the reader? If so, how is the accuracy comparison made apples-to-apples?
- **[Q7]** What is the mechanism by which adding a 64-expert router halves latency? A cost breakdown (router overhead vs downstream savings) would settle W3.
- **[Q8]** What happens to accuracy and latency as k and the expert count vary? Is 64 experts selected by validation or asserted?
- **[Q9]** What does "stable" mean quantitatively — what was the seed-to-seed range for each method?
- **[Q10]** Is code or a run artifact available? At minimum, the per-example predictions behind the reported numbers.

## Verdict

**Not ready for external submission; major revision required.** The paper has the shape of an evaluation (held-out split, multiple seeds, latency metric, compute-matched baseline) but not the substance: the headline comparison is under-powered by roughly an order of magnitude, the reported means are inconsistent with the stated evaluation design, the latency claim lacks a protocol and has an unexamined confound, and the SOTA claim has no external referent. These are not polish issues; W1–W3 each independently invalidate a headline claim, and W2 additionally raises a reporting-integrity question that must be resolved before the numbers can be trusted at all.

The revision path is tractable: the underlying experiment (router vs. matched baseline, accuracy plus latency, multiple seeds) is the right experiment. It needs a larger and identified evaluation set, variance reporting, a tuning-parity description, an ablation, and an honest latency protocol. Confidence in this assessment: **high** for W2 (arithmetic, verifiable), W6, and W8; **high** for W1 and W3 as stated-evidence gaps; **medium** for the severity of W4/W5/W7, which could be resolved by details the paper may simply have omitted rather than failed to do.

## Revision Plan

1. **Recompute and re-report all accuracy numbers (W2, W10).** Report integer per-seed counts, then mean ± 95% CI (or per-seed range) for each method. If the 0.1-point precision cannot be reproduced from the stated protocol, correct the protocol description or the numbers, and state which.
2. **Either substantiate or delete the SOTA claim (W1).** Name the benchmark, report at least two published baselines on the same split, and compare. If no external comparison exists, retitle the claim as "improves over a compute-matched internal baseline" everywhere, including the Abstract and Conclusion.
3. **Fix the latency protocol (W3).** Specify hardware, batch, context length, statistic, warm-up, repeats; report variance or a percentile. Add a cost breakdown separating router overhead from downstream savings, and state whether retrieval depth changes. If it does, report an accuracy-matched operating point.
4. **Enlarge the evaluation and report power (W2, W7).** Move to a split large enough that the minimum detectable difference is below the claimed effect, or explicitly frame the study as a pilot and drop inferential language.
5. **Describe baseline tuning parity (W4).** Architecture, shared components, search space, selection criterion, and the operational definition of "same budget."
6. **Add the router ablation (W5).** Uniform/fixed routing and random top-k at matched parameter count; sweep k and expert count.
7. **Report per-seed results and define "stable" (W6, Q9).** Replace the consistency claim with the actual seed spread.
8. **Document data provenance and contamination checks (W7).** Benchmark name, split construction, dedup procedure, and an explicit statement that the eval split was untouched during development.
9. **Add related work and a limitations section (W8, W11).** Position against sparsely-gated MoE and retrieval-routing work; state the 100-example and single-benchmark limitations explicitly.
10. **Complete the Method for reproducibility (W9).** Dataset/corpus size, batch size, sequence length definition, schedule, hardware, compute, and evidence that lr = 1e-4 was selected rather than defaulted.
11. **Soften the Conclusion (W11).** Replace the production-adoption recommendation with a scoped statement of what the evidence supports.

---

## Inline Annotations

> "We introduce SparseRoute, a routing layer for long-context retrieval. SparseRoute improves accuracy from 80.1% to 80.3% on our benchmark and is 2x faster. It establishes a new state of the art."

**[W1] FATAL:** "Our benchmark" is never named, and "state of the art" is asserted without a single external comparison. SOTA is a claim about the best published result on a defined task; the paper compares only to a baseline the authors trained. Delete or substantiate. See also **[W2]**: 80.1% and 80.3% cannot both be seed-means over 3 runs of a 100-example split.

> "SparseRoute adds a learned top-k router over 64 experts. We train for 10 epochs with Adam at a learning rate of 1e-4."

**[W5] MAJOR:** The router, the top-k selection, and the choice of 64 experts are three separable design decisions, none ablated and none justified. 64 is asserted, not selected. **[W9] MINOR:** Ten epochs, Adam, and one learning rate are not a reproducible training description — no batch size, sequence length, schedule, data size, hardware, or compute, and no indication that 1e-4 was tuned.

> "We evaluate on a held-out split of 100 examples from the benchmark."

**[W2] FATAL:** A 100-example split cannot resolve a 0.2-point difference; the binomial SE at p ≈ 0.8 is ≈ 4 points, so the claimed effect is ~1/20 of one SE. **[W7] MAJOR:** "The benchmark" is unnamed, the split construction is unspecified, and there is no dedup or contamination check against training passages — the dominant contamination channel for retrieval. **[Q3]** Was this split used for any design selection?

> "We compare against a baseline we trained ourselves with the same budget."

**[W4] MAJOR:** The baseline architecture is unidentified and "same budget" is undefined (epochs? FLOPs? wall-clock?). A baseline trained by the authors at one learning rate is not evidence of a tuned baseline. This is the single most common source of spurious small gains in routing papers.

> "We ran 3 seeds and the results were stable. We report mean accuracy over the seeds. We do not report confidence intervals or per-seed numbers."

**[W6] MAJOR:** "Results were stable" is a variance claim made while explicitly withholding all variance information. Per-seed numbers are the minimum needed to evaluate it. **[W2] FATAL:** These three sentences together make the reported means checkable — and they fail the check: the mean of 3 runs on 100 examples must land on a multiple of 1/300, so 80.1% and 80.3% are unreachable. The paper states the protocol that contradicts its own table.

> "| Baseline | 80.1% | 40 ms |" / "| SparseRoute | 80.3% | 20 ms |"

**[W3] FATAL:** Latency is given as bare single numbers with no hardware, batch size, context length, statistic, warm-up, or repeats. **[W10] MINOR:** Both accuracy values carry a tenth-of-a-point digit that the 100-example design cannot produce. **[Q1]/[Q5]** Request integer per-seed counts and the latency protocol.

> "SparseRoute improves accuracy by 0.2 points and halves latency. The gain is consistent across seeds."

**[W2]/[W6] FATAL:** "Consistent across seeds" is asserted with no per-seed data, and 0.2 points is 0.6 example predictions across all three seeds — far inside noise. **[W3] FATAL:** "Halves latency" restates an unprotocoled measurement. **[W5]** No ablation supports attributing either change to routing rather than to changed retrieval depth or added capacity.

> "SparseRoute is a new state of the art for efficient retrieval and should be adopted in production systems."

**[W11] MINOR (severity of claim: major):** A production-adoption recommendation from a 100-example offline evaluation with no cost model, failure analysis, or serving benchmark. Restate as a scoped claim about the internal comparison, and add a limitations section.

===== evals/README.md =====
# Research-quality evals

A small fixed eval for Feynman's research workflows. It runs `/lit` (or `/deepresearch`) on each question in `questions.jsonl`, then scores the artifacts with deterministic checks against arXiv, Crossref and doi.org. No LLM judge.

This directory is not in the npm package (`package.json` `files` does not list it).

## Rule

Run the eval before and after any change to prompts (`prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`), tools, extensions, or the Pi version. Use the same model and question ids for both runs, and commit both result files with the change.

## Run

Build first (`npm ci && npm run build`). Each question gets a fresh temp workspace and its own `FEYNMAN_HOME`, so your real `~/.feynman` is never read or written. The model's provider comes from a `models.json` that is copied into each isolated home. Example for an OpenAI-compatible gateway (the key is read from the environment and never written to disk):

```json
{
  "providers": {
    "ferrylane-openai": {
      "baseUrl": "https://gateway.ferrylane.ai/v1",
      "api": "openai-responses",
      "apiKey": "$FERRYLANE_API_KEY",
      "models": [
        { "id": "gpt-5.6-terra", "reasoning": true, "input": ["text"], "contextWindow": 400000, "maxTokens": 64000 }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

```sh
export FERRYLANE_API_KEY="$(cat ~/.ferrylane/api-key)"
node evals/run.mjs --model ferrylane-openai/gpt-5.6-terra --models-json /path/to/models.json \
  [--ids q01,q04] [--workflow lit|deepresearch] [--concurrency 2] [--timeout-min 45]
```

Built-in providers work the same way; pass their API key env var (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) and omit `--models-json`.

`--workflow deepresearch` sends one approval turn (`--continue`) after the plan gate. `--rescore evals/results/<file>.jsonl` re-scores the kept workdirs without rerunning Feynman, which is useful after a scorer change.

Output goes to `evals/results/<date>-<workflow>-<model>.jsonl` (one row per question: git SHA, dirty flag, Feynman version, scores, citation failures, usage, and the `workdir` (under `~/.cache/feynman-evals/` by default, `--work-root` to change) holding the full workspace, session JSONL and `feynman.log`) and a `.md` summary table.

## Scores

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `done` | A final `outputs/<slug>.md` exists with its `outputs/<slug>.provenance.md` sidecar. |
| `cites` | Distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs in the final output. |
| `valid` | Share of those identifiers that resolve (arXiv API `id_list`; Crossref, falling back to the doi.org handle API for non-Crossref DOIs). Lookups that fail on the network are left out. Unresolvable IDs are listed in `unresolved`. |
| `title` | Among resolved IDs with a known title, the share that match the output: the resolved title is at least 60% present (by word tokens) on a line that carries the ID, or, for author-year citations, the resolved first author's surname is on that line. Low values flag IDs attached to the wrong paper; see `title_mismatch`. Short-name citations ("When2Think, arXiv:…") also miss, so read the listed rows before calling something a hallucination. |
| `recall` | Share of the question's expected key papers that appear in the final output, by any listed identifier or by exact normalized title. 0 when there is no final output. |
| `wall`, `tokens`, `cost` | Wall time for the whole run, and token and cost totals summed over every Pi session file in the isolated home and temp dir (parent and subagent sessions, deduplicated). Cost is 0 when the provider's `models.json` entry has no `cost` block. |

The first baseline, `results/2026-09-23-lit-ferrylane-openai_claude-sonnet-5.*`, ran q01, q04, q07 and q10 on Feynman 0.5.0. It used `claude-sonnet-5` through the Ferrylane gateway because the gateway's GPT quota was exhausted that day.

Treat a single run as noisy. Compare before and after on the same ids, and look at the listed failures rather than only the percentages.

## Questions

`questions.jsonl` has 12 questions, each with expected key papers and a `source`:

- `q01`–`q06`: the six queries from Feynman's paper-discovery search benchmark (test-time compute, speculative decoding, sparse autoencoders, CRISPR base editing, mixture of experts, RAG).
- `q07`–`q09`: verbatim questions from LitQA2 ([futurehouse/lab-bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench), CC-BY-SA-4.0). The key paper is the item's `sources` DOI. These three items are redistributed under CC-BY-SA-4.0 with that attribution.
- `q10`–`q12`: hand-authored topics outside ML and biology (econometrics, weather forecasting, cosmology) whose key papers are unambiguous.

Keep the set fixed. Adding or editing a question breaks comparison with earlier result files; if you must, bump the question id instead of reusing one.

Next lanes, not built yet: ScholarQA-CS2 (AstaBench) citation precision and recall for `/lit`, DeepResearch Bench FACT for `/deepresearch`, and SciCoQA's 92 real paper–code discrepancies for `/audit` recall.

---
description: Run a literature review on a topic, lab, PI, or author using paper search and primary-source synthesis.
args: <topic-or-lab-or-author>
section: Research Workflows
topLevelCli: true
---
Investigate the following topic, lab, PI, or author as a literature review: $@

Derive a short slug from the topic (lowercase, hyphens, no filler words, ≤5 words). Use this slug for all files in this run.

## Workflow

1. **Plan** — Outline the scope: key questions, source types to search (papers, web, repos), time period, expected sections, and a small task ledger plus verification log. When the input appears to name a lab, PI, author, institution lab page, or author profile, run the review as a publication-corpus review: find the lab/author identity first, collect the reachable publication list, then map the research trajectory across that corpus. Write the plan to `outputs/.plans/<slug>.md`. Briefly summarize the plan to the user and continue immediately in the same turn with the next tool call; never end a turn with a message that only announces what you will do next. Do not ask for confirmation or wait for a proceed response unless the user explicitly requested plan review.
   - When updating the plan ledger later, keep edits small and valid. If an `edit` tool call fails with a JSON parse error or the replacement would require embedding a large markdown block, rewrite the full corrected plan file with the file-writing tool instead, then continue to final artifact/provenance verification.
2. **Gather** — Use the `researcher` subagent when the sweep is wide enough to benefit from delegated paper triage before synthesis. For narrow topics, search directly. Researcher outputs go to `outputs/.drafts/<slug>-research-*.md`. For publication-corpus reviews, the lead agent owns identity resolution and writes `notes/<slug>-publications.md` with reachable titles, years, venues, URLs/DOIs, and gaps before delegating trajectory synthesis. Prefer lab publication pages, author profiles, arXiv/OpenReview/Semantic Scholar pages, and paper search results that expose stable source URLs. Do not silently skip assigned questions; mark them `done`, `blocked`, or `superseded`.
   - For parallel researchers, write a workflow script that returns `await runs.all([...])` to `outputs/.plans/<slug>-workflow.js` with the write tool. In a later tool call, run `subagent` with `{ "workflow": "./outputs/.plans/<slug>-workflow.js", "async": true, "globalConcurrencyLimit": 4 }`. Each item has a unique `key`, an `agent`, and a short `task` naming its output path; items take no `output` field. Only `runs.all` is available; there is no `parallel()`.

     ```js
     return await runs.all([
       { key: "foundations", agent: "researcher", task: "Read outputs/.plans/<slug>.md and write outputs/.drafts/<slug>-research-foundations.md." },
       { key: "recent", agent: "researcher", task: "Read outputs/.plans/<slug>.md and write outputs/.drafts/<slug>-research-recent.md." },
     ]);
     ```
3. **Synthesize** — Separate consensus, disagreements, and open questions. For publication-corpus reviews, also identify 3-5 research trajectories and the 3-5 papers that most changed the corpus direction; rank them by contrastive originality, methodology strength, and relationship to prior art rather than by author prestige alone. When useful, propose concrete next experiments or follow-up reading. Use Mermaid diagrams for taxonomies, method pipelines, or lab trajectory maps when the structure is source-supported and changes the reader's research decision. Keep the output to research evidence, source coverage, and next research decisions; do not create non-research operational artifacts from a literature review run.
4. **Cite** — Spawn the `verifier` agent to add inline citations and verify every source URL in the draft.
5. **Verify** — Spawn the `reviewer` agent to check the cited draft for unsupported claims, logical gaps, zombie sections, and single-source critical findings. Fix FATAL issues before delivering. Note MAJOR issues in Open Questions. If FATAL issues were found, run one more verification pass after the fixes.
6. **Deliver** — Save the final literature review to `outputs/<slug>.md`. Write a provenance record alongside it as `outputs/<slug>.provenance.md` listing: date, sources consulted vs. accepted vs. rejected, verification status, and intermediate research files used; for publication-corpus reviews, include the publication-log path and unresolved corpus gaps. Before you stop, verify on disk that both files exist; do not stop at an intermediate cited draft alone.

# Dogfooding Feynman: an eval-quality case study of an AI research agent

**Harness:** Feynman 0.5.65 (released 2026-11-06)  
**Model:** `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`, thinking high  
**Session:** 2026-11-13, one session, `/work`  
**Status:** Complete, with explicit limitations. All probes were pre-registered before execution.

---

## Executive summary

I treated Feynman as both the object and the instrument of an evaluation. The result is a split verdict:

1. **The bundled research agents are strong.** Across two controlled verifier probes, the verifier caught **9 of 9** seeded citation/number defects with **0 false positives** on 4 valid claims. A researcher subagent refused a fabricated paper and documented a 10-source negative search without inventing an identifier. A reviewer caught the arithmetic impossibility in a deliberately underpowered evaluation paper.
2. **The instrument layer is weaker than the agents.** Crossref "DOI lookup" is implemented as a fuzzy `/works?query=` search. Three identifier-shaped queries returned unrelated records and no `not_found` signal; a non-existent DOI produced three unrelated papers and a `totalCount` of 16,049,765. `fetch_content` returns soft-404 placeholder pages as ordinary success.
3. **Feynman has a real eval harness — upstream, not in the release.** `evals/` contains 12 fixed questions, deterministic citation checks against arXiv/Crossref/doi.org, isolated homes and workspaces, git/version metadata, and before/after result files. It is excluded from the npm package.
4. **That eval harness is reproducible but narrow and currently ceilinged.** Across the six committed result files, `valid` is 100% on every completed question, `title` is 92–100%, and `recall` is 100% whenever a final output exists. The metrics discriminate completion, not research quality. The committed results stop at v0.5.3; the installed release is v0.5.65.
5. **Integrity is prompt-governed, not runtime-enforced.** Provenance sidecars are mandated by prompts, but no runtime check validates their contents. The eval's `done` metric only checks that a sidecar file exists. The direct-search path explicitly skips the verifier and reviewer, so the cheapest workflow gets the least independent checking.

The short version: **the evaluator is better than its instruments.** Feynman's prompts produce careful epistemic behavior; its tool contracts and runtime enforcement do not yet guarantee it.

---

## 1. What was tested

The case study has two halves:

- **Static audit** of the shipped harness: system prompt, agent definitions, workflow prompts, tool implementation, telemetry, package contents, and the upstream `evals/` directory.
- **Behavioral probes** using the harness itself: metadata lookup, negative-record handling, verifier defect detection, researcher non-existent-entity handling, reviewer eval critique, and URL-failure behavior.

The probe protocol and pass/fail rules were written to disk before execution:

- `experiments/feynman-eval-case-study/protocol.md`
- `experiments/feynman-eval-case-study/probe-outputs.md` (raw observations)
- Fixtures and outputs under `experiments/feynman-eval-case-study/`

The model was a flash-tier DeepSeek model, not a frontier model. That matters: the agent results below are a lower bound for what stronger models would do, and a warning that the harness's quality is model-dependent.

---

## 2. Feynman's own eval stack

### 2.1 What exists

The public repo contains `evals/`, which the npm package deliberately excludes. Its README describes "a small fixed eval for Feynman's research workflows" that runs `/lit` or `/deepresearch` on each question and scores artifacts "with deterministic checks against arXiv, Crossref and doi.org. No LLM judge." [S2]

The design is better than most agent repos:

| Property | Implementation |
|---|---|
| Fixed question set | 12 questions: 6 paper-discovery queries, 3 LitQA2 items, 3 hand-authored non-ML topics [S4] |
| Isolation | Fresh temp workspace and `FEYNMAN_HOME` per question; `FEYNMAN_TELEMETRY=0` [S3] |
| Determinism | Identifier extraction + arXiv/Crossref/doi.org resolution; no LLM judge [S3] |
| Versioning | Records git SHA, dirty flag, Feynman version, model, wall time, tokens, cost [S3] |
| Re-scoring | `--rescore` re-scores kept workdirs without rerunning the agent [S2] |
| Before/after | Committed pre/post result pairs around a prompt change [S6][S5] |

The before/after pair is the strongest evidence that the eval loop is real. Adding a `bg_wait` rule to `SYSTEM.md` moved the GPT run from **75% done** (q04 had no final provenance file) to **100% done**, while the other metrics stayed at their ceiling. The eval caught a real workflow regression. [S6][S5]

### 2.2 What the metrics actually measure

| Metric | Checks | Does not check |
|---|---|---|
| `done` | A final `outputs/<slug>.md` exists **and** a `.provenance.md` sidecar exists [S3] | Whether the sidecar is truthful or complete |
| `cites` | Count of distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs in the final text | Uncited claims; citation relevance |
| `valid` | Share of identifiers that resolve via arXiv, Crossref, or the doi.org handle API; network failures excluded [S2] | Whether the source supports the attached claim |
| `title` | At least 60% of the resolved title's word tokens appear on a line carrying the ID, or the first author's surname appears [S2] | Wrong number, wrong quote, wrong conclusion; short-name citations miss |
| `recall` | Expected key papers appear by ID or exact normalized title [S2] | Completeness beyond 1–2 key papers; precision |
| `wall`, `tokens`, `cost` | Usage summed over parent and subagent session files [S3] | `cost` is $0 when the model entry has no cost block [S2] |

That table is the central eval-quality finding. The harness measures **citation identity and workflow completion**, not **claim support**. A system can cite 40 real papers, attach every one to a false claim, and still score 100% `valid` and 100% `title`.

### 2.3 The ceiling problem

Across the six committed result files:

- `valid` is **100% on every completed question** in every run.
- `title` is **92–100%** on completed questions.
- `recall` is **100% whenever a final output exists**; 0 only when the run produced no output.
- `done` is the only metric with meaningful variance: **50%, 75%, 75%, 100%, 100%, 100%** across the runs I inspected. [S5][S6][S7][S8]

A metric that is 100% across six runs and three models is not discriminating research quality. It may be measuring something real — these models are good at citing resolvable papers — but it cannot tell a well-supported brief from a citation-laundered one. The README itself warns: "Treat a single run as noisy" and "look at the listed failures rather than only the percentages." [S2] The committed results do list failures: Claude q10 had a 93% title match with three wrong-paper attachments, which is exactly the kind of signal the metric can catch. [S7] But the aggregate table hides it behind a 97%.

There is also a **currency gap**. The committed results are dated 2026-09-23/24 and cover v0.5.0–0.5.3. The installed release is v0.5.65, dated 2026-11-06. The README's rule is to run the eval before and after any prompt, tool, or Pi-version change. The public evidence trail does not cover the current release. [S2][S16]

### 2.4 Cost of evaluation

The eval is not cheap. A 4-question GPT run used **13.4–14.1M tokens** and **~47 minutes** of wall time; the 4-question Sonnet baseline used **72.2M tokens** and **~2.2 hours**. [S5][S8] That is a reasonable price for a release gate, but it explains why the committed runs use 2–4 questions rather than all 12. It also means the eval is unlikely to be run by most users from the installed package, which is another reason the npm exclusion matters.

---

## 3. Dogfooding results

### 3.1 Identity and metadata: exact where the API is exact, fuzzy where it is not

| Probe | Expected | Observed | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| arXiv `1706.03762` | 2017, Vaswani, "Attention Is All You Need" | Exact match; 8 authors; 2017-06-12 [S9] | **Pass** |
| OpenAlex `W2626778328` | Same paper, 2017, Vaswani | Exact match; 136,211 citations [S14] | **Pass** |
| Crossref `10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762` | Exact DOI record | Top 3 unrelated DOI records; `totalCount` 6,599,726; no `not_found` | **Fail** |
| Crossref `10.9999/not.a.real.doi.2026` | Not found | Top 3 unrelated records; `totalCount` 16,049,765; no `not_found` | **Fail** |
| Crossref title `Attention Is All You Need Vaswani 2017` | 2017 NeurIPS record | Top 3 are 2025 `posted-content` records under DOI prefix `10.65215` | **Fail (identity)** |
| Semantic Scholar fabricated title | 0 results | `totalCount: 0`, no results [S25] | **Pass** |

The implementation explains the Crossref behavior: `searchCrossref` always builds `${CROSSREF_BASE}/works?query=...` and never uses the `/works/{doi}` endpoint. [S19] The tool description says "Crossref DOI metadata" and the parameter description says "identifier ... or DOI," so a model can reasonably expect an exact lookup and get a relevance-ranked keyword search instead. This is a **search/lookup conflation**, not a model hallucination.

The title query also surfaced a concrete data-quality hazard. The top record, `10.65215/r5bs2d54`, has the correct title, type `posted-content`, publisher "Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation," and creation date 2025-11-13. Its DOI resolution chain ends in a **404**:

`https://doi.org/10.65215/r5bs2d54` → 302 → `langtaosha.org.cn/index.php/lts/preprint/view/10` → 302 → `/lts/en/preprint/view/10` → 404.

A verifier that checks only "does Crossref have this title?" would attach a 2025 zombie DOI to a 2017 paper. Both verifier probes avoided it — the hard log explicitly says the `10.65215/*` records were "low-quality ... not used" — but the tool gave them no warning. [S27]

### 3.2 Verifier: 9/9 seeded defects, 0 false positives

I ran two controlled verifier probes.

**Coached probe.** The draft contained 5 seeded defects; the research notes explicitly recorded three of them as dead/unverifiable. The verifier:

| Defect | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Transformer attributed to 2019 | Corrected to 2017 |
| Fabricated Chen/Liu/Park paper + 41% + arXiv:2309.99999 | Removed; arXiv returned "no record" |
| GPT-3 95.2% zero-shot TriviaQA | Corrected to 64.3% zero-shot / 71.2% few-shot |
| Dead `example.com` survey + 68% | Removed; identified the IANA placeholder |
| "10x cheaper than RNNs" | Softened to the paper's qualitative claim |
| Valid: Transformer uses multi-head self-attention | Retained with citation |
| Valid: BERT uses MLM + NSP | Retained with citation |

Score: **5/5 defects, 0/2 false positives.** [S26]

**Hard probe.** The second draft had 4 defects and research notes that did **not** flag them. The verifier again caught all four: wrong Vaswani year (2019→2017), wrong GPT-3 number (95.2→64.3), unsupported 10x claim (removed), wrong Devlin year (2021→2019). It retained both valid claims, added NeurIPS and ACL Anthology venue records, and recorded its checks source by source. [S27]

The hard log is the most useful artifact of the whole session. It shows the verifier doing the right things:

- It noticed that Crossref is the wrong index for arXiv DOIs (`10.48550/*` is DataCite, not Crossref) and switched to OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar.
- It fetched the GPT-3 PDF and read Table 3.3 rather than trusting the abstract.
- It recorded the version discrepancy between the NeurIPS abstract (27.5/41.1 BLEU) and arXiv v7 (28.4/41.8 BLEU), and noted that no BLEU figure survived into the output, so the discrepancy did not affect a claim.
- It recorded Semantic Scholar HTTP 429, OpenAlex noise, and the `10.65215/*` spam records as limitations rather than silently using them.

I independently confirmed the NeurIPS-vs-arXiv BLEU discrepancy from the NeurIPS abstract page. [S10] The verifier's version note is accurate.

**Caveat.** The coached probe measures compliance with explicit notes more than independent discovery. The hard probe is the stronger evidence. Both use the same model; a different model may behave differently.

### 3.3 Researcher: a clean negative

The researcher was asked to verify a fabricated paper: "Sparse Tensor Routing for Low-Power Federated Learning" by Zhang, Okafor, and Lindqvist (2022).

It returned **"THE PAPER DOES NOT EXIST"** and refused to substitute an adjacent real paper. Its evidence table lists 10 sources across Semantic Scholar, arXiv, OpenAlex, Crossref, DBLP (blocked by an anti-bot challenge), and web search. It ran a control query (`ti:"federated learning"` → 3 entries) to prove the arXiv endpoint was working, distinguished direct API checks from indirect web checks, and stated the residual uncertainty: absence in open indexes is strong but not mathematically conclusive. [S28]

This is exactly the behavior the agent prompt asks for: "If a search returns zero results, the thing does not exist — do not invent it," and "URL or it didn't happen." [S21]

### 3.4 Reviewer: catches an eval that cannot support its own claim

I gave the reviewer a deliberately flawed 26-line paper with an evaluation claim: 80.1% → 80.3% on a 100-example split, 3 seeds, no CIs, self-trained baseline, no ablation, 2× latency, SOTA claim, production recommendation.

The reviewer caught every seeded flaw and added a quantitative catch I did not seed:

> The reported means, 80.1% and 80.3%, correspond to 240.3/300 and 240.9/300 — non-integer numerators, hence unattainable. Either the split is not 100 examples, or more than 3 runs are averaged, or the numbers were not produced by the described procedure.

It also computed the binomial standard error at p≈0.8, n=100 (≈4 points), noted the claimed 0.2-point gain is ~1/20 of one SE, and flagged the latency confound (routing may change retrieval depth, invalidating the accuracy comparison). [S29]

This is a genuine eval-quality critique, not a style review. The arithmetic check is verifiable: a mean of three runs on 100 examples must be a multiple of 1/300 ≈ 0.333 percentage points; 80.1% is 240.3/300 and 80.3% is 240.9/300.

### 3.5 Failure transparency: explicit errors are good; soft-404s are not

| URL | Observed behavior | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `https://doi.org/10.65215/r5bs2d54` | Explicit `HTTP 406: Not Acceptable` tool error with fallback advice | **Pass** |
| `https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.99999` | HTTP-200 page containing "There is no record..." | **Partial** — correct, but only if the reader reads the content |
| `https://example.com/2024-ml-evaluation-survey` | HTTP-200 IANA placeholder page | **Fail as a liveness check** |

The example.com case is the important one. The verifier prompt says "Verify every source URL — use fetch_content to confirm each URL resolves and contains the claimed content." [S20] A verifier that stops at "it resolved" would pass a placeholder page. The coached verifier did not: it read the page, recognized the IANA notice, and removed the claim. [S26] But the tool provides no content-integrity signal, so this depends on the model's diligence.

---

## 4. What this says about eval quality

### 4.1 The evaluator is better than its instruments

The agents' epistemic behavior is strong. The tools they rely on are not always identity-safe. This is a common pattern in agent evaluation: the prompt-level policy is good, but the measurement layer is a fuzzy search API, a URL fetcher that treats soft-404s as content, and a provenance contract that is not machine-checked.

For AI-eval quality, the lesson is to evaluate the **whole measurement chain**, not just the model's prose. A citation is only as good as the identifier resolution behind it; a "verified" label is only as good as the check that produced it.

### 4.2 Prompt-level integrity is not a system-level guarantee

Feynman's prompts are unusually explicit about provenance:

- The system prompt says every quantitative claim must trace to a source URL, research note, raw artifact path, or command output. [S23]
- The verifier prompt says to remove unsourced claims and verify meaning, not topic overlap. [S20]
- The `deepresearch` prompt requires a plan, draft, cited draft, verification, and provenance sidecar. [S19]

But the only runtime check is `wroteResearchOutput`, which scans `outputs/` and `papers/` for **any** recently modified file to set a telemetry boolean. [S18] There is no parser that checks the provenance sidecar's fields, no citation-support validator, and no gate that blocks delivery when verification is `BLOCKED`. The prompt says "use `Verification: BLOCKED`"; nothing enforces it.

The upstream eval inherits the same gap: `findFinal` requires a `.provenance.md` file to exist, but does not read it. [S3] A fabricated provenance file earns `done=yes`.

### 4.3 The direct-search path is the weakest link

`/deepresearch` has two modes:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Plan] --> B{Scale decision}
  B -->|direct: narrow question| C[Lead searches]
  C --> D[Lead drafts]
  D --> E[Lead self-cites and self-reviews]
  E --> F[Deliver + provenance]
  B -->|subagents: broad question| G[Researchers gather]
  G --> H[Lead drafts]
  H --> I[Verifier]
  I --> J[Reviewer]
  J --> F
  style E fill:#fee,stroke:#c00
```

In direct mode, the prompt says: "Do citation yourself" and "Do not spawn the `verifier` subagent for simple direct-search runs." [S19] That is a reasonable cost decision, but it means the most common cheap workflow has **no independent check**. The self-review is a conflict of interest: the agent that wrote the claim also decides whether it is supported.

The same pattern appears in `/lit`: the verifier and reviewer are spawned unconditionally in the prompt, but the agent can still skip them if subagents are unavailable. The prompt says "Use the `researcher` subagent when the sweep is wide enough" — another discretionary gate. [S22]

### 4.4 What a better eval would measure

The current eval measures citation identity, key-paper recall, and completion. A better eval for research quality would add:

1. **Claim-level support.** For each quantitative claim, check that the cited source contains the number/quote/conclusion. This is the failure mode my verifier probes target, and the current eval cannot see it.
2. **Negative controls.** Questions with no answer, fabricated papers, and dead URLs, scored on refusal and non-invention. The researcher probe shows the agent can do this; the eval does not test it.
3. **Provenance truth.** Parse the sidecar; check that the listed sources match the citations and that `Verification:` is consistent with the checks.
4. **Discriminative power.** Report the distribution across runs, not just means. A metric at 100% across six runs is a ceiling, not a result.
5. **Coverage.** Run all 12 questions, or state which subset and why. The committed results cover 2–4.
6. **Cost honesty.** Report $0 only when the provider truly costs $0; otherwise mark cost unavailable. [S2]

---

## 5. Recommendations for Feynman

Prioritized by eval-quality impact per unit of change:

**P0 — Make identifier lookup exact or explicitly fuzzy.**
Add `crossref_get_work:DOI` using `https://api.crossref.org/works/{doi}` and return a `not_found` field for identifier-shaped queries. Do not silently fall back to `/works?query=`. The current behavior turns a non-existent DOI into three unrelated papers. [S19]

**P0 — Detect soft-404s in `fetch_content`.**
Return a content-integrity flag when the page is a known placeholder domain (example.com, parked pages), a "no record" page, or a title/entity mismatch. The verifier prompt already asks for meaning-level checks; the tool should make them cheap. [S20]

**P1 — Machine-check provenance.**
Add a validator that parses the sidecar, confirms every inline `[N]` maps to a source, and marks `Verification: PASS/BLOCKED` only when the underlying checks are present. Use it in the eval's `done` metric. This closes the gap between "a sidecar exists" and "the sidecar is true." [S3][S18]

**P1 — Require independent verification in direct mode, scaled to the claim.**
For a one-paragraph answer, a single verifier pass over the final claims is cheap. For a full brief, keep the current verifier + reviewer. The current binary (direct = no independent check) is the wrong tradeoff for an integrity-first agent. [S19]

**P1 — Publish eval results with each release, and cover all 12 questions.**
The current public results stop at v0.5.3. Add a release-gate summary (even a 4-question smoke run) to `RELEASES.md`, and state the subset. The eval is already deterministic and committed; the missing piece is currency. [S2][S16]

**P2 — Add claim-level and negative-control probes to the eval.**
Seed a known wrong number and a fabricated citation into a fixture, and score whether the verifier removes them. This is the same design I used here; it is cheap and directly measures the failure mode the current metrics miss.

**P2 — Report uncertainty and ceiling.**
Add per-question rows to the summary (already in JSONL), and a note when a metric is at 100% across all runs. The README already says single runs are noisy; the table should say when a metric cannot discriminate. [S2]

**P2 — Reduce duplicate tool output.**
OpenAlex returns the same work in both `results` and top-level fields, and arXiv returns `records` and `results`; this inflates context. Not an integrity bug, but it makes long research runs more expensive. [S14]

---

## 6. Threats to validity

- **N = 1 session, one model, one date.** The agent results are a lower bound and may not generalize to frontier models or other providers.
- **The fixtures were authored by the harness itself.** This is dogfooding bias. Mitigation: the protocol and scoring rules were written before execution, the hard verifier probe did not leak the defects in its notes, and raw outputs are saved.
- **The coached verifier probe is easier than the hard probe.** I report them separately and weight the hard probe more heavily.
- **The reviewer probe uses an intentionally flawed paper.** It measures whether the reviewer can catch seeded eval-quality flaws, not whether it reviews real papers well.
- **The upstream eval harness was not executed.** Running it requires a repo build and provider quota; this case study audits the code and the committed results, not a fresh run. That is a `not run` item, not a `pass`.
- **Crossref data changes.** The `10.65215/*` records may be removed or changed; the observation is dated 2026-11-13 and saved in `upstream/crossref-10.65215-r5bs2d54.json`.
- **Telemetry audit is static.** I inspected the code paths but did not capture a live PostHog payload. The claim that prompts/model output are excluded is supported by the `$ai_generation` property list, not by a network capture. [S18]

---

## 7. Open questions

1. Does the hard-verifier performance hold on a frontier model, and on a model with a smaller context window?
2. What is the verifier's false-positive rate on obscure but valid citations, especially non-English and non-DOI sources?
3. Would the upstream eval still show 100% `valid` on the full 12 questions at v0.5.65, or is the ceiling an artifact of the 4-question subsets?
4. Can a provenance validator be strict enough to catch fabricated sidecars without rejecting legitimate multi-source briefs?
5. How much does the direct-mode self-check cost in accuracy versus a verifier pass? A paired A/B on the same drafts would answer this.
6. Does the `10.65215/*` Crossref pollution affect other classic papers, or is it specific to this title? A small sample of 20 classic papers would quantify the hazard.

content.text:
# Dogfooding Feynman: an eval-quality case study of an AI research agent

**Harness:** Feynman 0.5.65 (released 2026-11-06)  
**Model:** `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`, thinking high  
**Session:** 2026-11-13, one session, `/work`  
**Status:** Complete, with explicit limitations. All probes were pre-registered before execution.  
**Verification:** PASS WITH NOTES — behavioral probes completed; the upstream eval harness was audited from code and committed results but not re-executed.

---

## Executive summary

I treated Feynman as both the object and the instrument of an evaluation. The result is a split verdict:

1. **The bundled research agents are strong.** Across two controlled verifier probes, the verifier caught **9 of 9** seeded citation/number defects with **0 false positives** on 4 valid claims. A researcher subagent refused a fabricated paper and documented a 10-source negative search without inventing an identifier. A reviewer caught the arithmetic impossibility in a deliberately underpowered evaluation paper.
2. **The instrument layer is weaker than the agents.** Crossref "DOI lookup" is implemented as a fuzzy `/works?query=` search. Three identifier-shaped queries returned unrelated records and no `not_found` signal; a non-existent DOI produced three unrelated papers and a `totalCount` of 16,049,765. `fetch_content` returns soft-404 placeholder pages as ordinary success.
3. **Feynman has a real eval harness — upstream, not in the release.** `evals/` contains 12 fixed questions, deterministic citation checks against arXiv/Crossref/doi.org, isolated homes and workspaces, git/version metadata, and before/after result files. It is excluded from the npm package.
4. **That eval harness is reproducible but narrow and currently ceilinged.** Across the six committed result files, `valid` is 100% on every completed question, `title` is 92–100%, and `recall` is 100% whenever a final output exists. The metrics discriminate completion, not research quality. The committed results stop at v0.5.3; the installed release is v0.5.65.
5. **Integrity is prompt-governed, not runtime-enforced.** Provenance sidecars are mandated by prompts, but no runtime check validates their contents. The eval's `done` metric only checks that a sidecar file exists. The direct-search path explicitly skips the verifier and reviewer, so the cheapest workflow gets the least independent checking.

The short version: **the evaluator is better than its instruments.** Feynman's prompts produce careful epistemic behavior; its tool contracts and runtime enforcement do not yet guarantee it.

---

## 1. What was tested

The case study has two halves:

- **Static audit** of the shipped harness: system prompt, agent definitions, workflow prompts, tool implementation, telemetry, package contents, and the upstream `evals/` directory.
- **Behavioral probes** using the harness itself: metadata lookup, negative-record handling, verifier defect detection, researcher non-existent-entity handling, reviewer eval critique, and URL-failure behavior.

The probe protocol and pass/fail rules were written to disk before execution:

- `experiments/feynman-eval-case-study/protocol.md`
- `experiments/feynman-eval-case-study/probe-outputs.md` (raw observations)
- Fixtures and outputs under `experiments/feynman-eval-case-study/`

The model was a DeepSeek v4.1 Flash model. That matters: the agent results below may not generalize to other models, and they are a reminder that harness quality is model-dependent.

---

## 2. Feynman's own eval stack

### 2.1 What exists

The public repo contains `evals/`, which the npm package excludes. Its README describes "a small fixed eval for Feynman's research workflows" that runs `/lit` or `/deepresearch` on each question and scores artifacts "with deterministic checks against arXiv, Crossref and doi.org. No LLM judge." [S2]

The design is unusually concrete for an agent repo:

| Property | Implementation |
|---|---|
| Fixed question set | 12 questions: 6 paper-discovery queries, 3 LitQA2 items, 3 hand-authored non-ML topics [S4] |
| Isolation | Fresh temp workspace and `FEYNMAN_HOME` per question; `FEYNMAN_TELEMETRY=0` [S3] |
| Determinism | Identifier extraction + arXiv/Crossref/doi.org resolution; no LLM judge [S3] |
| Versioning | Records git SHA, dirty flag, Feynman version, model, wall time, tokens, cost [S3] |
| Re-scoring | `--rescore` re-scores kept workdirs without rerunning the agent [S2] |
| Before/after | Committed pre/post result pairs around a prompt change [S6][S5] |

The before/after pair is the strongest evidence that the eval loop is real. Adding a `bg_wait` rule to `SYSTEM.md` moved the GPT run from **75% done** (q04 had no final provenance file) to **100% done**, while the other metrics stayed at their ceiling. The eval caught a real workflow regression. [S6][S5]

### 2.2 What the metrics actually measure

| Metric | Checks | Does not check |
|---|---|---|
| `done` | A final `outputs/<slug>.md` exists **and** a `.provenance.md` sidecar exists [S3] | Whether the sidecar is truthful or complete |
| `cites` | Count of distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs in the final text | Uncited claims; citation relevance |
| `valid` | Share of identifiers that resolve via arXiv, Crossref, or the doi.org handle API; network failures excluded [S2] | Whether the source supports the attached claim |
| `title` | At least 60% of the resolved title's word tokens appear on a line carrying the ID, or the first author's surname appears [S2] | Wrong number, wrong quote, wrong conclusion; short-name citations miss |
| `recall` | Expected key papers appear by ID or exact normalized title [S2] | Completeness beyond 1–2 key papers; precision |
| `wall`, `tokens`, `cost` | Usage summed over parent and subagent session files [S3] | `cost` is $0 when the model entry has no cost block [S2] |

That table is the central eval-quality finding. The harness measures **citation identity and workflow completion**, not **claim support**. A system can cite 40 real papers, attach every one to a false claim, and still score 100% `valid` and 100% `title`.

### 2.3 The ceiling problem

Across the six committed result files in `evals/results/`: [S31]

- `valid` is **100% on every completed question** in every run.
- `title` is **92–100%** on completed questions.
- `recall` is **100% whenever a final output exists**; 0 only when the run produced no output.
- `done` is the only metric with meaningful variance: **50%, 75%, 75%, 100%, 100%, 100%** across the runs I inspected. [S5][S6][S7][S8]

A metric that is 100% across six runs and three models is not discriminating research quality. It may be measuring something real — these models are good at citing resolvable papers — but it cannot tell a well-supported brief from a citation-laundered one. The README itself warns: "Treat a single run as noisy" and "look at the listed failures rather than only the percentages." [S2] The committed results do list failures: Claude q10 had a 93% title match with three wrong-paper attachments, which is exactly the kind of signal the metric can catch. [S7] But the aggregate table hides it behind a 97%.

There is also a **currency gap**. The committed results are dated 2026-09-23/24 and cover v0.5.0–0.5.3. The installed release is v0.5.65, dated 2026-11-06. The README's rule is to run the eval before and after any prompt, tool, or Pi-version change. The public evidence trail does not cover the current release. [S2][S16]

### 2.4 Cost of evaluation

The eval is not cheap. A 4-question GPT run used **13.4–14.1M tokens** and **42–47 minutes** of wall time; the 4-question Sonnet baseline used **72.2M tokens** and **~2.2 hours**. [S5][S8] That is a reasonable price for a release gate, but it explains why the committed runs use 2–4 questions rather than all 12. Inference: few users will run it from the installed package, which makes the npm exclusion matter for external auditability.

---

## 3. Dogfooding results

### 3.1 Identity and metadata: exact where the API is exact, fuzzy where it is not

| Probe | Expected | Observed | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| arXiv `1706.03762` | 2017, Vaswani, "Attention Is All You Need" | Exact match; 8 authors; 2017-06-12 [S9] | **Pass** |
| OpenAlex `W2626778328` | Same paper, 2017, Vaswani | Exact match; 136,211 citations [S14] | **Pass** |
| Crossref `10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762` | Exact DOI record | Top 3 unrelated DOI records; `totalCount` 6,599,726; no `not_found` | **Fail** |
| Crossref `10.9999/not.a.real.doi.2026` | Not found | Top 3 unrelated records; `totalCount` 16,049,765; no `not_found` | **Fail** |
| Crossref title `Attention Is All You Need Vaswani 2017` | 2017 NeurIPS record | Top 3 are 2025 `posted-content` records under DOI prefix `10.65215` | **Fail (identity)** |
| Semantic Scholar fabricated title | 0 results | `totalCount: 0`, no results [S25] | **Pass** |

The implementation explains the Crossref behavior: `searchCrossref` always builds `${CROSSREF_BASE}/works?query=...` and never uses the `/works/{doi}` endpoint. [S19] The tool description says "Crossref DOI metadata" and the parameter description says "identifier ... or DOI," so a model can reasonably expect an exact lookup and get a relevance-ranked keyword search instead. This is a **search/lookup conflation**, not a model hallucination.

The title query also surfaced a concrete data-quality hazard. The top record, `10.65215/r5bs2d54`, has the correct title, type `posted-content`, publisher "Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation," and creation date 2025-11-13. Its DOI resolution chain ends in a **404**:

`https://doi.org/10.65215/r5bs2d54` → 302 → `langtaosha.org.cn/index.php/lts/preprint/view/10` → 302 → `/lts/en/preprint/view/10` → 404.

A verifier that checks only "does Crossref have this title?" would attach a 2025 zombie DOI to a 2017 paper. Both verifier probes avoided it — the hard log explicitly says the `10.65215/*` records were "low-quality ... not used" — but the tool gave them no warning. [S27]

### 3.2 Verifier: 9/9 seeded defects, 0 false positives

I ran two controlled verifier probes.

**Coached probe.** The draft contained 5 seeded defects; the research notes explicitly recorded three of them as dead/unverifiable. The verifier:

| Fabricated Chen/Liu/Park paper + 41% + arXiv:2309.99999 | Removed; arXiv returned "no record" |
| GPT-3 95.2% zero-shot TriviaQA | Corrected to 64.3% zero-shot / 71.2% few-shot |
| Dead `example.com` survey + 68% | Removed; identified the IANA placeholder |
| "10x cheaper than RNNs" | Softened to the paper's qualitative claim |
| Valid: Transformer uses multi-head self-attention | Retained with citation |
| Valid: BERT uses MLM + NSP | Retained with citation |

Score: **5/5 defects, 0/2 false positives.** [S26]

**Hard probe.** The second draft had 4 defects and research notes that did **not** flag them. The verifier again caught all four: wrong Vaswani year (2019→2017), wrong GPT-3 number (95.2→64.3), unsupported 10x claim (removed), wrong Devlin year (2021→2019). It retained both valid claims, added NeurIPS and ACL Anthology venue records, and recorded its checks source by source. [S27]

The hard log is the most useful artifact of the whole session. It shows the verifier doing the right things:

- It noticed that Crossref is the wrong index for arXiv DOIs (`10.48550/*` is DataCite, not Crossref) and switched to OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar.
- It fetched the GPT-3 PDF and read Table 3.3 rather than trusting the abstract.
- It recorded the version discrepancy between the NeurIPS abstract (27.5/41.1 BLEU) and arXiv v7 (28.4/41.8 BLEU), and noted that no BLEU figure survived into the output, so the discrepancy did not affect a claim.
- It recorded Semantic Scholar HTTP 429, OpenAlex noise, and the `10.65215/*` spam records as limitations rather than silently using them.

I independently confirmed the NeurIPS-vs-arXiv BLEU discrepancy from the NeurIPS abstract page. [S10] The verifier's version note is accurate.

**Caveat.** The coached probe measures compliance with explicit notes more than independent discovery. The hard probe is the stronger evidence. Both use the same model; a different model may behave differently.

### 3.3 Researcher: a clean negative

The researcher was asked to verify a fabricated paper: "Sparse Tensor Routing for Low-Power Federated Learning" by Zhang, Okafor, and Lindqvist (2022).

It returned **"THE PAPER DOES NOT EXIST"** and refused to substitute an adjacent real paper. Its evidence table lists 10 sources across Semantic Scholar, arXiv, OpenAlex, Crossref, DBLP (blocked by an anti-bot challenge), and web search. It ran a control query (`ti:"federated learning"` → 3 entries) to prove the arXiv endpoint was working, distinguished direct API checks from indirect web checks, and stated the residual uncertainty: absence in open indexes is strong but not mathematically conclusive. [S28]

This is exactly the behavior the agent prompt asks for: "If a search returns zero results, the thing does not exist — do not invent it," and "URL or it didn't happen." [S21]

### 3.4 Reviewer: catches an eval that cannot support its own claim

I gave the reviewer a deliberately flawed 26-line paper with an evaluation claim: 80.1% → 80.3% on a 100-example split, 3 seeds, no CIs, self-trained baseline, no ablation, 2× latency, SOTA claim, production recommendation.

The reviewer caught every seeded flaw and added a quantitative catch I did not seed:

> The reported means, 80.1% and 80.3%, correspond to 240.3/300 and 240.9/300 — non-integer numerators, hence unattainable. Either the split is not 100 examples, or more than 3 runs are averaged, or the numbers were not produced by the described procedure.

It also computed the binomial standard error at p≈0.8, n=100 (≈4 points), noted the claimed 0.2-point gain is ~1/20 of one SE, and flagged the latency confound (routing may change retrieval depth, invalidating the accuracy comparison). [S29]

This is a genuine eval-quality critique, not a style review. The arithmetic check is verifiable: a mean of three runs on 100 examples must be a multiple of 1/300 ≈ 0.333 percentage points; 80.1% is 240.3/300 and 80.3% is 240.9/300.

### 3.5 Failure transparency: explicit errors are good; soft-404s are not

| URL | Observed behavior | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `https://doi.org/10.65215/r5bs2d54` | Explicit `HTTP 406: Not Acceptable` tool error with fallback advice | **Pass** |
| `https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.99999` | HTTP-200 page containing "There is no record..." | **Partial** — correct, but only if the reader reads the content |
| `https://example.com/2024-ml-evaluation-survey` | HTTP-200 IANA placeholder page | **Fail as a liveness check** |

The example.com case is the important one. The verifier prompt says "Verify every source URL — use fetch_content to confirm each URL resolves and contains the claimed content." [S20] A verifier that stops at "it resolved" would pass a placeholder page. The coached verifier did not: it read the page, recognized the IANA notice, and removed the claim. [S26] But the tool provides no content-integrity signal, so this depends on the model's diligence.

## 4. What this says about eval quality

### 4.1 The evaluator is better than its instruments

The agents' epistemic behavior is strong. The tools they rely on are not always identity-safe. The pattern matters for AI-eval quality: the prompt-level policy is good, but the measurement layer is a fuzzy search API, a URL fetcher that treats soft-404s as content, and a provenance contract that is not machine-checked.

For AI-eval quality, the lesson is to evaluate the **whole measurement chain**, not just the model's prose. A citation is only as good as the identifier resolution behind it; a "verified" label is only as good as the check that produced it.

### 4.2 Prompt-level integrity is not a system-level guarantee

Feynman's prompts are unusually explicit about provenance:

- The system prompt says every quantitative claim must trace to a source URL, research note, raw artifact path, or command output. [S23]
- The verifier prompt says to remove unsourced claims and verify meaning, not topic overlap. [S20]
- The `deepresearch` prompt requires a plan, draft, cited draft, verification, and provenance sidecar. [S19]

But the only runtime check related to output provenance is `wroteResearchOutput`, which scans `outputs/` and `papers/` for **any** recently modified file to set a telemetry boolean. [S18] There is no parser that checks the provenance sidecar's fields, no citation-support validator, and no gate that blocks delivery when verification is `BLOCKED`. The prompt says "use `Verification: BLOCKED`"; nothing enforces it.

The upstream eval inherits the same gap: `findFinal` requires a `.provenance.md` file to exist, but does not read it. [S3] A fabricated provenance file earns `done=yes`.

### 4.3 The direct-search path is the weakest link

`/deepresearch` has two modes:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Plan] --> B{Scale decision}
  B -->|direct: narrow question| C[Lead searches]
  C --> D[Lead drafts]
  D --> E[Lead self-cites and self-reviews]
  E --> F[Deliver + provenance]
  B -->|subagents: broad question| G[Researchers gather]
  G --> H[Lead drafts]
  H --> I[Verifier]
  I --> J[Reviewer]
  J --> F
  style E fill:#fee,stroke:#c00
```

In direct mode, the prompt says: "Do citation yourself" and "Do not spawn the `verifier` subagent for simple direct-search runs." [S19] That is a reasonable cost decision, but it means the most common cheap workflow has **no independent check**. The self-review is a conflict of interest: the agent that wrote the claim also decides whether it is supported.

The same pattern appears in `/lit`: the prompt tells the agent to spawn the verifier and reviewer, but nothing in the runtime verifies that the spawn occurred. The prompt also says "Use the `researcher` subagent when the sweep is wide enough" — another discretionary gate. [S22]

### 4.4 What a better eval would measure

The current eval measures citation identity, key-paper recall, and completion. A better eval for research quality would add:

1. **Claim-level support.** For each quantitative claim, check that the cited source contains the number/quote/conclusion. This is the failure mode my verifier probes target, and the current eval cannot see it.
2. **Negative controls.** Questions with no answer, fabricated papers, and dead URLs, scored on refusal and non-invention. The researcher probe shows the agent can do this; the eval does not test it.
3. **Provenance truth.** Parse the sidecar; check that the listed sources match the citations and that `Verification:` is consistent with the checks.
4. **Discriminative power.** Report the distribution across runs, not just means. A metric at 100% across six runs is a ceiling, not a result.
5. **Coverage.** Run all 12 questions, or state which subset and why. The committed results cover 2–4.
6. **Cost honesty.** Report $0 only when the provider truly costs $0; otherwise mark cost unavailable. [S2]

## 5. Recommendations for Feynman

Prioritized by eval-quality impact per unit of change:

**P0 — Make identifier lookup exact or explicitly fuzzy.**
Add `crossref_get_work:DOI` using `https://api.crossref.org/works/{doi}` and return a `not_found` field for identifier-shaped queries. Do not silently fall back to `/works?query=`. The current behavior turns a non-existent DOI into three unrelated papers. [S19]

**P0 — Detect soft-404s in `fetch_content`.**
Return a content-integrity flag when the page is a known placeholder domain (example.com, parked pages), a "no record" page, or a title/entity mismatch. The verifier prompt already asks for meaning-level checks; the tool should make them cheap. [S20]

**P1 — Machine-check provenance.**
Add a validator that parses the sidecar, confirms every inline `[N]` maps to a source, and marks `Verification: PASS/BLOCKED` only when the underlying checks are present. Use it in the eval's `done` metric. This closes the gap between "a sidecar exists" and "the sidecar is true." [S3][S18]

**P1 — Require independent verification in direct mode, scaled to the claim.**
For a one-paragraph answer, a single verifier pass over the final claims is cheap. For a full brief, keep the current verifier + reviewer. The current binary (direct = no independent check) is the wrong tradeoff for an integrity-first agent. [S19]

**P1 — Publish eval results with each release, and cover all 12 questions.**
The current public results stop at v0.5.3. Add a release-gate summary (even a 4-question smoke run) to `RELEASES.md`, and state the subset. The eval is already deterministic and committed; the missing piece is currency. [S2][S16]

**P2 — Add claim-level and negative-control probes to the eval.**
Seed a known wrong number and a fabricated citation into a fixture, and score whether the verifier removes them. This is the same design I used here; it is cheap and directly measures the failure mode the current metrics miss.

OpenAlex returns the same work in both `results` and top-level fields, and arXiv returns `records` and `results`; this inflates context. Not an integrity bug, but it makes long research runs more expensive. [S14]

## 6. Threats to validity

- **N = 1 session, one model, one date.** The agent results are a lower bound and may not generalize to frontier models or other providers.
- **The fixtures were authored by the harness itself.** This is dogfooding bias. Mitigation: the protocol and scoring rules were written before execution, the hard verifier probe did not leak the defects in its notes, and raw outputs are saved.
- **The coached verifier probe is easier than the hard probe.** I report them separately and weight the hard probe more heavily.
- **The reviewer probe uses an intentionally flawed paper.** It measures whether the reviewer can catch seeded eval-quality flaws, not whether it reviews real papers well.
- **The upstream eval harness was not executed.** Running it requires a repo build and provider quota; this case study audits the code and the committed results, not a fresh run. That is a `not run` item, not a `pass`.
- **Crossref data changes.** The `10.65215/*` records may be removed or changed; the observation is dated 2026-11-13 and saved in `upstream/crossref-10.65215-r5bs2d54.json`.
- **Telemetry audit is static.** I inspected the code paths but did not capture a live PostHog payload. The claim that prompts/model output are excluded is supported by the `$ai_generation` property list, not by a network capture. [S18]

---

## 7. Open questions

1. Does the hard-verifier performance hold on a frontier model, and on a model with a smaller context window?
2. What is the verifier's false-positive rate on obscure but valid citations, especially non-English and non-DOI sources?
3. Would the upstream eval still show 100% `valid` on the full 12 questions at v0.5.65, or is the ceiling an artifact of the 4-question subsets?
4. Can a provenance validator be strict enough to catch fabricated sidecars without rejecting legitimate multi-source briefs?
5. How much does the direct-mode self-check cost in accuracy versus a verifier pass? A paired A/B on the same drafts would answer this.
6. Does the `10.65215/*` Crossref pollution affect other classic papers, or is it specific to this title? A small sample of 20 classic papers would quantify the hazard.

187:### 4.2 Prompt-level integrity is not a system-level guarantee

241:## 5. Recommendations for Feynman
---

1. **Claim-level support.** For each quantitative claim, check that the cited source contains the number/quote/conclusion. This is the failure mode my verifier probes target, and the current eval cannot see it.
2. **Negative controls.** Questions with no answer, fabricated papers, and dead URLs, scored on refusal and non-invention. The researcher probe shows the agent can do this; the eval does not test it.
3. **Provenance truth.** Parse the sidecar; check that the listed sources match the citations and that `Verification:` is consistent with the checks.
4. **Discriminative power.** Report the distribution across runs, not just means. A metric at 100% across six runs is a ceiling, not a result.
5. **Coverage.** Run all 12 questions, or state which subset and why. The committed results cover 2–4.
6. **Cost honesty.** Report $0 only when the provider truly costs $0; otherwise mark cost unavailable. [S2]

### 4.5 Telemetry: metadata-only by design, with an error-text boundary

The extension captures five event families: session start, workflow start, tool use, `$ai_generation`, and workflow completion. `$ai_generation` includes model, provider, token counts, cache counts, latency, HTTP status, and stop reason, but explicitly no `$ai_input` or `$ai_output_choices`; tool arguments and prompts are not captured. [S18]

The exception is error text. `error_message` and `pi_stderr` are sent raw up to 4,000 characters, with only the home directory replaced by `~`. [S18] The README's "never sends ... paper content" promise therefore depends on tool error messages not containing paper text; the code does not classify or redact content. This is a policy boundary, not an observed leak. It is the kind of boundary an eval-quality review should state explicitly rather than infer from a privacy claim.

---

## 5. Recommendations for Feynman

Prioritized by eval-quality impact per unit of change:

**P0 — Make identifier lookup exact or explicitly fuzzy.**
Add `crossref_get_work:DOI` using `https://api.crossref.org/works/{doi}` and return a `not_found` field for identifier-shaped queries. Do not silently fall back to `/works?query=`. The current behavior turns a non-existent DOI into three unrelated papers. [S19]

**P0 — Detect soft-404s in `fetch_content`.**
Return a content-integrity flag when the page is a known placeholder domain (example.com, parked pages), a "no record" page, or a title/entity mismatch. The verifier prompt already asks for meaning-level checks; the tool should make them cheap. [S20]

**P1 — Machine-check provenance.**
Add a validator that parses the sidecar, confirms every inline `[N]` maps to a source, and marks `Verification: PASS/BLOCKED` only when the underlying checks are present. Use it in the eval's `done` metric. This closes the gap between "a sidecar exists" and "the sidecar is true." [S3][S18]

**P1 — Require independent verification in direct mode, scaled to the claim.**
For a one-paragraph answer, a single verifier pass over the final claims is cheap. For a full brief, keep the current verifier + reviewer. The current binary (direct = no independent check) is the wrong tradeoff for an integrity-first agent. [S19]

**P1 — Publish eval results with each release, and cover all 12 questions.**
The current public results stop at v0.5.3. Add a release-gate summary (even a 4-question smoke run) to `RELEASES.md`, state the subset, and cover all 12 questions across a release cycle rather than in one expensive run. The eval is already deterministic and committed; the missing piece is currency. [S2][S16]

**P2 — Add claim-level and negative-control probes to the eval.**
Seed a known wrong number and a fabricated citation into a fixture, and score whether the verifier removes them. This is the same design I used here; it is cheap and directly measures the failure mode the current metrics miss.

**P2 — Report uncertainty and ceiling.**
Add per-question rows to the summary (already in JSONL), and a note when a metric is at 100% across all runs. The README already says single runs are noisy; the table should say when a metric cannot discriminate. [S2]

**P2 — Reduce duplicate tool output.**
OpenAlex returns the same work in both `results` and top-level fields, and arXiv returns `records` and `results`; this inflates context. Not an integrity bug, but it makes long research runs more expensive. [S14]

---
